zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). This review supplies its own scan-based transcription decisions and English notes; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

lines.note: This is a mid-quotation continuation: even the person's manner was refined and gracious. The supplied preceding scan does not contain its beginning, so no missing antecedent is invented. Taif. is the chosen reading of the damaged source label; its final f remains less secure than the rest of the line.

The Portuguese begins with the person's physiognomy and facial features. Preserve the historical filosomia wording. The damaged second numeral has an open curved trace, read as 0 in Lib. 20.; the faint mark above the e in feiçoẽs is retained as a tilde. Both small details remain nonblocking uncertainties, not modernized reconstructions.

runs.text: erão eminentes, & atè a condição era muito

lines.note: The facial features were outstanding, and even the person's disposition was very noble. Condição concerns manner or character here, matching the Japanese continuation above.
Noble and agreeable completes the description of the person's disposition. This closes the carried-over quotation before the new mimegurashi entry.
Mimegurashi means looking around by moving the eyes. Its aita principal part is the historical s-verb form, not a missing modern shita ending.
Os olhos completes 'looking around with the eyes'. The short line is body continuation, not an independent label.
Mimeguri is looking around while going about. The source distinguishes bodily movement here from simply casting one's eyes around in the preceding entry.

Mimyoo is explained by kidoku naru koto, something miraculous or marvelous. The upward-pointing circumflex is visible on enlargement, correcting OCR Mimiǒ; the supplied NINJAL headword independently agrees with Mimiô. Milagrosa is divided at the physical line end.
Grosa completes milagrosa; maravilhosa supplies the alternative 'marvelous'. This ends the mimyoo gloss before the separate word mimi, ear.
Mimi is an ear. Mimi ga akanu begins an idiomatic explanation of not understanding or not being willing to listen, with the Portuguese negative carried into the next row.

runs.text: entender, ou não querer ouuir por ſer rude, ou

lines.note: The refusal or failure to listen is attributed to lack of understanding or stubbornness. The damaged vowel supports rude, not OCR rade; the second alternative is completed below.
Teimoso completes the previous alternative. Mimi ga naru describes ringing in the ears; preserve the historical Portuguese Zonirem rather than modernizing its vowel.
Orelhas completes the ringing gloss. Mimi ga tsubururu means becoming deaf, with ensurdecer divided across the next physical break.

runs.text: decer. ¶ Permet. Não entender por rude,

lines.note: Decer completes ensurdecer. The figurative extension is not understanding through lack of comprehension; the compressed Permet. label is retained unexpanded.
The figurative failure to understand may have another cause. Mimi tsubure then begins a noun phrase for a deaf person, followed by an alternative form.
Mimi no tsubureta hito is a person whose hearing has failed. The Portuguese gives both deafness and the extended sense of a person unable to grasp things.

runs.text: que não percebe as couſas por rudeza, &c.

lines.note: The figurative person does not perceive matters through dullness. This completes the preceding alternative rather than introducing a new hearing verb.

Mimi ni sasayaku is whispering into someone's ear, glossed as speaking privately. The Japanese sense and the long-s types support ſaſayaqu rather than OCR faſayaqu; the omitted opening pilcrow is restored from the scan.
Mimi wo sumasu means listening attentively. The Portuguese directly supplies the attentive-listening sense, not a literal cleaning of the ear.
Mimi wo tozuru or fusagu gives two ways of closing or blocking one's ears. The lower-case l introduces the alternative, and Fechar continues into its object below.

runs.text: as orelhas, ou não querer ouuir. ¶

lines.note: The idiom also means refusing to listen. The following Mimi- starts another example and must remain physically divided from uo below.
Mimi wo odorokasu is being startled by something heard. The printed initial v belongs to the historical spelling and is not normalized to o.
Cousa completes the startling-hearing gloss. Mimi wo koyasu begins the image of satisfying or enriching the ears with pleasant things heard.
The ears are satisfied by hearing good and pleasing things. This completes the idiomatic explanation of koyasu rather than adding another independent definition of mimi.
Mimi ni iru is something entering the ears or becoming audible or intelligible. The Portuguese phrase continues with the body-part object below.
The alternative gloss is making oneself understood. Mimi wo starts the following ear-refreshing idiom and remains on this physical row.
Mimi wo susugu is explained as refreshing the hearing through good things heard. Preserve the printed susugu form and the continuation into the objects below.
Pleasant things complete the refreshing-hearing gloss. Mimi wo kaku then shifts to physically picking or cleaning the ears, translated on the next line.
The Portuguese describes picking or scraping the ears. This is the explanation of mimi wo kaku, not an additional Japanese entry.
Mimiaka and mimi no aka are two expressions for dirt or wax in the ears. The lowercase l is the alternative marker, not part of the headword.
Orelhas completes 'dirt of the ears'. This short continuation closes the wax entry before the ear-pick implement.
Mimikaki is the implement for picking or cleaning the ears. The Portuguese agent/instrument noun refers to the tool in this context.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe ent ende bem, ou

lines.note: Mimichikai describes something readily understood. The tight but visible internal spacing in ent ende is retained from the aligned draft, not silently regularized to modern word spacing.
The alternative says that the thing is perceived immediately. It reinforces the intelligibility sense of mimichikai, rather than proximity in physical distance.

runs.text: O latejarem os ouuidos, ou ma-

lines.note: Mimidare concerns throbbing ears or discharge from them. The Portuguese mana(r) construction begins at ma- and continues below.
Nar completes manar, the flowing of matter from the ears. The repeated Japanese word starts Mimida-, not the garbled OCR Mumnida-, and continues into rega below.
Mimidare ga aru means having this ear condition. The source's ter esta doença confirms that the divided word is the same noun as the headword.

runs.text: Couſa que ſe não entende bem.

lines.note: Mimidooi is something not readily understood. The printed douoi vowel sequence is preserved rather than normalized to a modern long-vowel spelling.
Mimidooi kotowari ja describes an explanation or argument that is hard to understand. Arrezo- begins the Portuguese arrazoamento-type noun across the line boundary.
Amento completes the noun for a discourse or argument. The relative clause says that it is poorly understood, matching the preceding Japanese example.
Mimidoona is the corresponding adjectival variant and refers back to the same difficult-to-understand sense. The dictionary's na ending is retained.
Mimigawarake is a small earthenware lid or dish of a particular shape. The raised, rounded terminal mark is read as a comma rather than the OCR hyphen; its impression is weak.
The alternative Portuguese description is an earthenware basin or bowl. This completes the shape-based utensil definition.
Mimigashimashii concerns a noisy commotion that affects the ears. The Portuguese relative clause continues into what is heard or found troublesome.

runs.text: ſente nos ouuidos, ou moleſta aos que ouuem.

lines.note: The noise is felt in the ears or troubles those hearing it. This gives the unpleasant auditory force of the preceding adjective.
Mimijikai is again something easily understood. The voiced spelling gicai is printed and should not be assimilated to the earlier chicai headword.
Entender completes the easy-understanding gloss. The related mimijikana form follows at the head of the next column.
Mimijikana refers back to the easily understood sense at the foot of column 1. It is an adjectival variant, not a continuation of the preceding line's Portuguese infinitive.

runs.text: Pedras que ſe poem na borda da

lines.note: Mimiishi are stones laid at the edge of paving. The definition continues with their position and their strengthening function, rather than referring to stones in an ear.
The edge stones strengthen or hold the other stones of the pavement. The final outras takes pedras as its noun on the next row.
Pedras completes the explanation of the retaining border stones. This very short body continuation is distinct from the following ear-wax entry.
Mimi no aka is dirt or wax in the ears. Mi- starts the repeated expression in an example of removing it, rather than an independent use of the honorific prefix.

runs.text: mino acauo caqu. l, mimiuo caqu.

lines.note: Mimi no aka wo kaku or mimi wo kaku gives two expressions for cleaning the ears. The Portuguese A- begins alimpar on the next row.
Limpar completes alimpar, the historical prefixed verb for cleaning. It is not silently reduced to modern limpar by dropping the previous line's A-.

runs.text: Ponta da orelha na parte in-

lines.note: Mimi no biku denotes the lower tip or lobe of the ear. In- begins inferior, specifying the lower rather than upper part.
Ferior completes inferior and thus the location of the earlobe. The physical line is retained despite consisting of only the end of a word.
Miminoha is a regional word for ears. The upright X. is the source's regional label, not part of the Portuguese noun or the Japanese headword.

The gloss denotes the root or attachment of the ears. Mimi no ne is lexically expected and is the supplied NINJAL reading, but this impression has an abraded, u-like type with no secure upper n bridge. The baseline ue is therefore retained as a nonblocking glyph uncertainty, not interpreted as proof of an ear-upper-part meaning. The printed arreigadadas spacing is also preserved.
Mimikiki is someone who hears well. Item introduces an additional sense of quickly understanding what is said.
The second sense is a person who immediately grasps the reason or argument. The historical spacing arezão is preserved.

Mimitsuku is a nocturnal owl. Cami here is a regional designation within the Portuguese explanation, not the religious word in the preceding page's candle entry; the regional alternative follows below.

The source says the form used in Cami is mimizuku. Printed diz corrects OCR dix; Mimizzucu is an upright Japanese word embedded in this Portuguese statement and is eligible for whole-word typeface review.
Mimitoi hito is a person quick to hear or apprehend. The Portuguese subject phrase is continued by the hearing and perception verbs below.

runs.text: ouue, ou percebe depreſſa. ¶ Item, permet.

lines.note: The person hears or perceives quickly. Item, permet. then marks a figurative extension to intellectual understanding rather than merely auditory acuity.

runs.text: Homem que entende depreſſa, & penetra as

lines.note: The figurative sense is someone who understands quickly and penetrates matters. The final article as belongs to cousas on the next row.
Cousas completes the description of a perceptive person. This one-word continuation remains body text, not a heading or label.

runs.text: O ouuir bem, ou perceber de preſſa

lines.note: Mimitoshi denotes hearing well or perceiving quickly. The historical toshi form and the printed separation de preſſa are retained.
The object is some thing perceived quickly. The final upright S. identifies written usage and is distinguished from the Portuguese gloss.
Mimishii is becoming deaf. The printed abbreviated forms ijte and ijta are retained, and Verb. introduces the grammatical qualification on the next row.
Defect. completes the label for a defective verb. The scan has the abbreviation and its stop, not the OCR's extra final i in defecti.
Mimizu means earthworms. The simple Portuguese plural makes this an independent animal-name entry rather than another auditory derivative.
Mimizugata is a raised welt from a whip or blow. The final stop is visible and restores punctuation omitted by the OCR; the entire definition occupies this one row.
Mimochi here is conduct, deeds, or one's way of life. Mi- begins the example of reforming that conduct on the next row.
Mimochi wo aratamuru means reforming one's conduct. The Portuguese emendar a vida states that moral or behavioral sense directly.
The second mimochi entry means pregnancy. Kano onna begins the example 'that woman', with the pregnancy expression divided across the line boundary.
Mimochi ni natta and mimochi de gozaru are alternative ways of saying she has become or is pregnant. A- begins aquella in the translation below.

runs.text: quella molher està prenhe. Palaura de molheres.

lines.note: The woman is pregnant. The dictionary labels the Japanese expression as women's speech; this sociolinguistic comment is preserved as the source's description, not generalized beyond it.
Mimochina describes a pregnant woman. The na form is printed as its own headword with a short nominal Portuguese explanation.
Mimon is explained by imada kikazu, not yet heard. It denotes something unheard, distinct from the preceding pregnancy vocabulary.

runs.text: Mimon fuqen, l, mimon fuqenna fi-

lines.note: Mimon fuken and the adjectival phrase mimon fuken na hito describe someone neither heard of nor seen. Fi- is the beginning of hito, not an independent abbreviation.

runs.text: Homem que nunca vi, nem ouui delle.

lines.note: To completes fito. The Portuguese specifies a man whom the speaker has never seen and of whom the speaker has never heard.
Mimonai describes something without substance, empty, or insignificant. Preserve the historical sustancia spelling without supplying a modern b and retain the tilde on the second a of vaã.
De pouco momento completes the sense 'of little importance'. Momento here concerns consequence or weight, not a short duration.
Mimonasa is the nominal derivative, lack of substance or significance. Its indentation groups it with the preceding adjective rather than making it a new full gloss.
Mimonoo is the corresponding adverbial form. The caron is visible and is not replaced by an unmarked o or by the vowel in the following independent mimono entry.

runs.text: Couſa pera ſe ver, como couſa fermo-

lines.note: Mimono is something worth seeing, such as an attractive sight. Fermo- starts the adjective fermosa, which continues below.
Sa completes fermosa, and lustrosa adds brilliance or splendor. The line completes the appealing-spectacle gloss rather than describing the next act of turning to look.
Mimuki means looking by turning one's face. The printed u and uita are abbreviated principal forms and are retained without adding the stem.

runs.text: Certa baga cõ que tingẽ de roxo.

lines.note: Mimurasaki is a berry used to dye purple. The source does not establish a botanical species here; the nasal abbreviations cõ and tingẽ are preserved.
Mina means everything or everyone. Mina ni naru introduces the idiom of something being used up completely, explained below.
The thing comes to an end or is exhausted. The gloss explains the idiomatic effect of mina ni naru, not merely a change into a collective group.
Minakami is a source or headwater. The example begins with that source becoming muddy; nigot- is the first part of nigotte across the physical break.
Minakami nigotte nagare kiyokarazu says that when the source is muddy the stream is not clear. Tur- starts the Portuguese turva, divided into the next row.

runs.text: ua, a corrente tambem não ſera limpa. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Ua completes turva, and the Portuguese states that the current likewise will not be clean. Item begins another sense that continues on the next supplied page; the separate Princi- below is a catchword, not another body row.
